1.blurb: Heian Japan tells the Genpei War from the doomed court's side, and this chapter gives the full naval account of Dan-no-ura — the tidal reversal that turned the fight, the betrayal that exposed the Taira flagship, and the drowning of the child-emperor Antoku with the imperial sword.

Heian Japan's Genpei War chapter follows Yoshitsune's dazzling winning campaigns in full — the cliff descent at Ichinotani, the storm crossing to Yashima — the victories that made him one of Japan's most beloved tragic heroes before his brother turned on him.

4.blurb: Mongol Empire tells the invasions from the attacker's side: Kublai building a Chinese-style empire he named the Yuan, and launching against Japan what it calls the largest naval operation in pre-modern history — the same two fleets this chapter sees broken on the beaches of Hakata Bay.

Mongol Empire's chapter on Kublai and the Yuan narrates how the grandson of Genghis Khan conquered China and proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in 1271, the empire that would send its envoys and then its armies against the islands.

7.blurb: Mongol Empire shows where this humbling title came from: Kublai Khan had addressed his 1268 ultimatum to the 'King of Japan,' demanding tributary submission to China — the very framework Yoshimitsu would later accept from Ming China for the sake of trade.

12.blurb: Edo Japan carries the payoff of the Christian century that begins here: Xavier's 1549 landing, the hundreds of thousands of converts and Christian daimyō, and then the savage purge — the expulsion edicts, the fumi-e tests, and the Shimabara Rebellion.

Edo Japan follows the Portuguese black ships (kurofune) from this trading age into the closed-country age — the same word later attached to Perry's vessels in 1853 — and tells how the open era of European contact was finally sealed shut.

13.blurb: Joseon Korea tells Hideyoshi's invasions from the side that bore the devastation: the Imjin War, the scorched peninsula, and Admiral Yi Sun-sin's armored turtle ships shattering the Japanese fleets — among the proudest chapters of Korea's own story.

Ming Dynasty covers the third party to the war: the Ming armies that poured into Korea to defend their tributary, turning Hideyoshi's planned conquest of China into a grinding stalemate that drained all three states.

Edo Japan develops where these 1597 crucifixions led: the systematic suppression of Christianity under the Tokugawa, from the 1614 expulsion edict to the Shimabara Rebellion and the near-total eradication of the faith.

14.blurb: Edo Japan opens on the same battlefield and carries the story forward: the road to Sekigahara, the noon defection of Kobayakawa Hideaki, and how Ieyasu's victory became the 250-year Tokugawa peace this medieval age gives way to.

Edo Japan gives William Adams's full arc — the Dutch ship Liefde wrecked on the Kyushu coast in 1600, and his life as Ieyasu's adviser on Western affairs — set inside the story of Japan closing its doors to all of Europe but one Dutch trading post.

Edo Japan is the sequel to this whole story: the long, locked-down, astonishingly stable peace under the Tokugawa shoguns that the closed door created, beginning right where Sekigahara and the 1603 shogunate leave off.
